[i]Chicago[/i] is an exhilerating piece of work. Incredibly cynical about celebrity, tabloid journalism, lawyers, circus trials, and what happens when they mix, it holds no punches in its portrayal of shallow people whose main concern is numero uno. It is also filled with bravura performances from it's three stars, Renee Zellwegger, Catherine Zeta Jones, and Richard Gere. The music numbers are beautifully photgraphed, the choreography by director Rob Marshall is first rate, and it all comes together spectacularly in the film's grand finale. The rebirth of the musical is complete, as we certainly have here a musical classic for the 21st century.

I sat down with Chi-town and flat-chested Renee for a second viewing tonight, and was kinda taken aback at the fact that I fell asleep halfway through it. You could blame the double Whopper and Hi-C that I just ingested prior to watching it (I AM THE BURGER KING!), but that doesn't do Latifah's heaving bosom any critical good.
 
So the problem, I figured out, is the nagging feeling that led me to grading the movie an A- instead of a good ol' A the first time around. This time, it was more glaring: the actors for the most part don't know how to sell [i]it[/i]. [i]It[/i] is that certain sumthin'-sumthin' that keeps musical theater alive and tappin' (and no, not the refined gay population of New York City). It's not the smokey lights nor the shiney black stage. It's in the body - in the curl of the finger, the notch of the ankle, and the blink of a wink. It's finishing a move as if every eye is on you and you want to stretch the moment into an epoch unto yourself (good, Lord, I've gone all second-person in this review).
 
Zeta-Woman comes closest to it, and durned if she doesn't rob the marshall out from under her leads' noses. But watch the individual numbers of the performers, there's something inauthentic and mimic-y about their presence on stage, and their discomfort hurts the heartbeat of the satire. Rob Marshall obviously meant to capture the almost grassroots Vaudevillian feel of the solitary actor owning an actual stage - but these screen actors are simply at a loss without the world of the movie to inhabit. It's like they're on the outside looking in for the spark of the theater to set us, the audience, off - too bad it's a film that's separating us from them.

Broadway musicals lose something when committed to celluloid. There is an energy in live performance that connects with the audience, a breaking down of the fourth wall that leads audience members to feel like they are part of the show. Its electric and, often, impossible to duplicate on film. Chicago has long been one of Broadways most popular musicals because it is big and bold; it draws you in and never lets go. Not so with the film version. Although Rob Marshall does a very admirable job bringing Chicago to life on the big screen, it ultimately left me feeling disconnected and dispassionate.

What was most surprising about Chicago were the musical performances of the three primary leads: Renee Zellweger, Catherine Zeta-Jones, and Richard Gere. Zellweger was terrifically vampy as Roxie Hart, the murderess with stars in her eyes who comes to view her crime as a way to make a name for herself. Although her vocalizations were sometimes on the thin side, she displayed wonderful range and proved to be a pretty good hoofer, too. Zeta-Jones was a bit less convincing as Velma Kelly, the slightly hard-bitten performer who kills her cheating husband and sister just moments before going on stage for a rousing rendition of All That Jazz. Zeta-Jones singing voice was a nice contrast to Zellwegers: low and somewhat dusky although, tonally, sometimes flat. Zeta-Jones is also an amazing dancer and really shines on the number I Cant Do It Alone. Richard Gere also does a fine job as Billy Flynn, the lawyer in the middle. Gere has a nice voice and will astound you with his tap dance number late in the film.

The musical numbers are beautifully staged. The editing is sometimes too quick, but theres never any doubt that the actors are doing their own foot and vocal work. Queen Latifah performs a red-hot version of When Youre Good To Mama. Cell Block Tango is sexy and sensual as each woman sings about the crime that landed her in prison. We Both Reached For The Gun is a fantastically staged visual of the way Flynn is attempting to control Roxies image in the press. Zellweger does a slinky cross between Monroe and Harlow during the memorable Roxie. The musical highlight, however, comes from supporting cast member John C. Reilly as Roxies dim-witted husband. His poignant rendition of Mr. Cellophane is touching and emotional; it was the only time in the film where the 4th wall came crashing down and I truly felt something for one of these characters.

Chicago was nominated for 13 Academy Awards last year and won 6, including Best Picture. Im not sure that I would agree. Chicago is a fine film  if musicals appeal to you.

[u][i]Chicago[/i] (Rob Marshall, 2002)[/u] 
For a movie about murder and media manipulation and corruption in the justice system, [b]Chicago[/b] isn't very edgy. Though it's based on Bob Fosse's 1975 Broadway musical, which was alleged to be a very smart, ahead-of-its-time satire, all scalding wit appears to have been cooled, all sharp corners filed down to better suit the tastes of Oscar voters taking in this splashy, ingratiating end-of-the-year Miramax production.
 
That's not to say that [i]Chicago[/i] isn't entertaining - maybe even satisfying - on a bright, spangly, facile level; it's just not the original, revolutionary movie musical it's being hailed as. With high calibre Hollywood stars like Renée Zellweger, Catherine Zeta-Jones, and Richard Gere decked out in fabulous, resplendent costumes (a slinky silver number and golden locks for Zellweger, short-cropped black hair and dress for Zeta-Jones, a straw boater and sharp suit for Gere), it's a simple, old-fashioned pleasure just to watch these three sing and shimmy and hoof it up on screen. (Zellweger's got a voice as thin and slight as her physical structure, while Zeta-Jones has a more voluptuous, full-bodied oral presence.) But it's obvious that moral darkness and dramatic inventiveness are low on the agenda for this windy city musical. And [i]Chicago[/i]'s director, Rob Marshall, isn't nearly the wizard that Baz Luhrmann - whose [i]Moulin Rouge[/i] was the raging, glorious, absinthe-soaked musical that really revolutionized the cinematic form - is.
 
In the early '20s, Roxie Hart (Zellweger) is a blond cutie pie who dreams of fame and fortune. Tired of her dullsville marriage, she starts up a fling with a guy who promises to help her reach her goals; upon learning he's a liar and a leech, she shoots him point blank in a fit of rage. This lands her on Murderess Row, a prison cell block of impassioned women who similarly deep-sixed their husbands and lovers, led by a large and in-charge Queen Latifah (a.k.a. Mama the prison warden). To justify what they did, the women leap up in their cells, singing and slinking to the "Cell Block Tango", which runs down the list of the women's motives. 
 
Their reasons, to put it mildly, are quite petty, including those of Velma Kelly (Zeta-Jones), the vampish vaudeville star who's Roxie's idol and who wields a cigarette as though it were an extra limb. Velma's cunning strategy for getting away with it is to team up with Billy Flynn (Gere), a scheming lawyer who has never lost a case of a woman accused of murder. Roxie also receives Billy's aid, once her betrayed husband (John C. Reilly, perhaps the deepest persona in this flashy circus) puts up the money, of course. Billy's got a plan to help Roxie: He'll transform her into a tabloid star, knowing her bad-girl charisma will let her off the hook.
 
Each of these actors gets a rousing, bouncy John Kander-Fred Ebb song to sink their teeth into, of course. Zeta-Jones sets the scene with her sensational performance of "All That Jazz". Queen Latifah shakes her bodacious booty and practically growls the lyrics to "When You're Good to Mama". John C. Reilly is beautifully melancholy in his rendition of "Mr. Cellophane". And Gere and Zellweger's showstopper is a number that mimmicks a press conference where Zellweger is a puppet whose talk and movements are all manipulated by puppet master Gere. 
 
But the performances essentially add up to nothing more than these songs, lively as they are; they never really get under the skin of the characters. Certainly Zellweger could use more meat on the bones of her simplistically cuddly character. Zeta-Jones is more robust, but still basically coasts on her rich voice and trendy flapper hair. I tire of Gere's faux-breezy, all-smiles, charming-huckster shtick. Only Reilly brings a hint of substance to his sympathetic role as Roxie's neglected mechanic husband, a tribute to the actor's surprising versatility. 
 
The direction also has an old-style lack of originality. Marshall does little more to the sets than flood them with traditional red and blue light. The movie's look feels simple and almost elemental, and Marshall is certainly no visual wizard. And yes, this is another one of those female empowerment movies, this time the women being empowered by, of all things, manslaughter. 
 
None of my quibbles and quarrels about lack of depth and originality may matter in the long run, though. [i]Chicago[/i] is just warm and glossy and entertaining enough to be a born crowd pleaser, and just easygoing and inoffensive enough to be born Oscar bait. It is good old-fashioned entertainment, but far from the great, fresh, edgy, revolutionary movie it so desperately wants to be. No matter, though: To the Academy, the commonplace is timeless. [b]B[/b]

[b][font=Verdana][size=2]CHICAGO (2002)

[/b][u]THE GOOD:

[/u]--The musical numbers in this film are truly astounding. They are brilliantly choreographed, wonderfully filmed and the actors do terrific jobs. Each musical number is filled with vibrant, kinetic energy; all use colours to great effect. I was impressed with how well Rob Marshall built everything up, I've never seen a movie by this guy before and he really has excellent skill. It shows in the way he utilises everything and anything to his bargain, and his talent for bringing mood and atmosphere to all these wonderfully constructed sets and musical numbers.

--Bill Condon's script tremendously captures the essence of scandalous Hollywood. This is shown most successfully through Roxie Hart's story. This girl rises and falls in a number of different ways. In the beginning she is a sweet, cute little button with charming aspirations for fame. By the end of the film, she is frankly a kanniving little bitch who'll stop at nothing to receive money, power and fame. This isn't random at all; it's crafted very well and absolutely believable given the circumstances. It was massively entertaining and often hysterically funny seeing how Roxie Hart and Velma Kelly came up with new ways to get the press's attention, I especially loved Roxie's cry of "I hope the fall didn't hurt the baby!"

--This film isn't filled with the best cast, you might say. Renee Zellweger is probably one of the only really reliable actresses in the film. I mean, think about it, Catherine Zeta-Jones has never been very accomplished as an actress, she failed dismally in films like "The Haunting" and "Entrapment". Richard Gere is all right, but he's never been that popular with audiences and critics. Well, you'll forget all about that while watching this movie. Zellweger predictably turns in a top-form performance; she is just delightful in the role. Gere is also razzle-dazzle terrific, he somehow brings across warmth in this sleazy, unlikeable role. There aren't many actors who can do that. Zeta-Jones is the real shining star of the film, she is simply INCREDIBLE. Her performance is the most energetic of the film and Zeta-Jones does step a foot wrong. I was so completely convinced by her that I totally forgot I was watching an actressshe WAS Velma Kelly, through and through. Queen Latifah is also excellent, proving big is beautiful and showing her comedic range. All the actors are actually really good singers too; I loved how they all used their real voicesvery cool.

--"Chicago" has a bit of everything and will probably be enjoyed by the majority of audiences. It has quite a bit of comedy, a lot of music and beat, energy a-go-go, even a little bit of dramatic empathy in places. It's an all-round film; it's hard to think of any audience (of age or choice) who wouldn't enjoy it.

[u]THE BAD:

[/u]--"Chicago" slows down a little towards the end. The musical numbers are as awesome as ever, but the courtroom scenes have a tendency to be a tiny bit repetitive and some scenes felt like 'lets get through this dialogue part so we can move on to the next musical number.' Rarely I felt this way, but it still has to be mentioned.

--Lucy Liu's role in the film is completely pointless and serves no purpose in the film other than to give Roxie another reason to be a star. This is very obvious and it's a waste of a potentially very good performance from Liu (what screen-time she has features some great acting from the "Charlie's Angels" star).

[u]RATING:

[/u]9/10 - Not quite as strong as last year's "Moulin Rouge", "Chicago" remains one exhilarating funny honey that left me cheering.

 Im pretty sure Im all alone in my feelings that this film didn't deserve any sort of recognition, but there you have it.  I do not think it is a terrible film or anything, just not a very good one.  first, I strongly disagree with Polanskis directorial choice of shooting many of the horrors committed in the Warsaw Ghetto from the Szpilmans POV. It adds an air of clinical and dispassionate scientific observation to the film that dilutes the drama and emotion of the scenes. Take for example the incident of the man in the wheel chair being thrown to his death, and latter his family being gun down by the Nazis. we never see their faces; we never see the Nazis faces; we never see anything in intimate detail, as such it seems like an study of the event, but not a drama.  that scene is a horrible, but not gut-wrenching like it should have been.  Now, I understand Polanski shooting some stuff like this; after it makes sense from a character POV, and prevents the film from being overtly depressing and heavy handed. But not most of it as there is not a single scene that is gut-wrenching, even through a few should have been.  I strongly think that Polanskis direction makes the film a moving history lesson, instead of a gripping human drama.  this brings me to my second big point; the film is so relentlessly conventional, and single minded that it ends up being a just Holocaust movie. now that doesnt make it inherently a bad movie; indeed the Holocaust is filled with millions of stories worth telling, but it does limit it from being great.  The Pianist brings nothing new to the table, and does nothing to set it apart from things like the Diary of Anne Frank, Maus, or Schindlers List.  thats basically why I think it deserved no sort of recognition.  
 
 Gangs of New York
 
 I really understand why people would hate this movie.  there are some many obvious story telling problems that the term flawed has to be used.  lets see a fairly useless voice over narration that basically only adds un-dramatized exposition? check, and to make matters worse there are some scenes that I cant figure out why the exposition was needed beyond atmosphere. ( i.e types of thieves, not voiceover but the fight over being called a chiseler and all it variants. not the fight, but the lines over what chiseler means totally unneeded exposition.) a central plot that is both cliché and overpowered by the numerous subplots? totally check. to me this is the biggest problem, the revenge tale/love triangle is well boring; it is a tale that has played out before, and been told better before countless times. the subplots (and/or episodes) of racism, Tweed, Irish, corruption, the draft ect. all mar it more because they are more interesting, and better told.  The film overstuffs itself; the relative strength of the central narrative is out matched by the subplots.  Furthermore, the ending is a bit anti-climatical.  there are other problems like Diaz sheer inability to do an Irish accent, or sometimes act in general or how Scorsese several times throughout the course of the film looses his grip on the narrative. (some may argue unneeded plot twists, as well, such as the election, but I do not hold the viewpoint)
 
 and yet, I cant help loving the film. I think when Boss Tweed showed up for the first time I knew right there and then I loved the film. (when he mentioned the courthouse later on I nearly had a heart attack)  I love history, and the New York gang lore of the Civil War through the progressive era is some of the most interesting historical stuff I know of.  GONY does a good job at presenting much of the gang lore faithful to the spirit, and some of the time to the letter.  (through the dates are screwed up big time for some stuff, i.e Monk lived in 1910, and Bill died in 1858 [I think]) More importantly, I strongly feel the film captures perfectly most of the issues, causes and feelings that lead to the draft riots and other problems that Civil war and Post Civil-War America faced.  GONY captures so much, and so well, of the conditions of New York city during this time frame that I prefer to think of it as a character study of the elements that led to gangs forming in the first place.  I really do think the film should have been called Streets of New York  Finally, the production design is masterful, and captures the 5 corners just right .  Also, I think Day-Lewis should have won for Bill, easily the best performance of that year.
 
 Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
 
 again, while I hate judging the LOTR apart from each other, I think TTT is stronger than FOTR, on the whole, but weaker than ROTK, on the whole. so, Im glad King was the one to win.  again impressive production values, a finely written screenplay that does the impossible, and a director that brings it to life with such force that it demand attention make TTT a great film. (the EE for my money  is better through, same for FOTR)  
 
 the main reason why Im glad this didnt win BP is of the three it is the one that stands the least alone.  FOTR and King stand nearly, but not quite, alone.  Furthermore, my two biggest problems with all of LOTR is in TTT, those being the hackneyed Legolas sliding down the stairs during Helms Depp and the false drama of (through I understand why they did this, and I really cant think of a much better solution) Striders little tumble off the cliff. (through on the flip side of my two favorite moments are in TTT as well, those being the Last March of the Ents and storming of Isengard.)
 
 The Hours
 
 first, this film is about how art effects life, and the pains of conformity. (and some other things) I say this because usually when I defend it people question me on its themes.  Second, holy cow what a well acted film this is. Kidman, Moore and Streep are positively amazing, and Im astonished at how subtle Moore was. I am butter in theirs hand ever time I watch this film, Kidman is a worthy winner, through I wish it went to Renee; and yes I have seen Far from Heaven, I wasnt that impressed with Moore there.. the rest of the actors are quite good as well, and Harris gives quite a performance.  Third, the screenplay is amazing simple how it makes internal conflicts external in subtext.  For the longest time I never thought any work connected to Virginia Wolf, but bio-pics, would turn out great because much of her work is pure internal, which is something films dont do as well as say a novel.  Really, between Hares fine screenplay, and Daldrys use of image systems (food for example) the Hours becomes a film layered with subtle subtext that dramatize the internal in some of the best ways I have ever seen.   The Hours really is writing, directing and acting combining to make film that is deeply moving. ultimately, I think the film is uplifting btw.
 
 Chicago
 
 I saw this film 12 times in the theater.  I have never done that before (Gosford Park I saw on DVD for the first time), and I cant imagine doing so again any time soon.  Chicago was a huge surprise for me because my sister hates the stage show, and we usually agree on things like this. (it turns out that it became her favorite movie of all time) anyway, this film is a snappy, energy filled, and rousing musical with some serious teeth and is extremely clever. I think a lot more clever than people realize.  First Condons screenplay, besides have snappy, processing endlessly quotable dialog, makes the Chicago material fresh, while solving a problem that has stump many others.  the songs in Chicago are very different from other musicals. they for example are not driving the plot forward, or furthering the characters relationships the way songs traditionally do; they comment on the plot, therefore are apart from it.  Furthermore, none of the songs are out and out book numbers, meaning songs that occur between two characters. Thus the songs are between singer and audience, or are innately theatrical. this problem was solved by having the songs occur in Roxies head.  I think for that solution alone Condon should have won.  by having the songs fantasies Chicago adds another layer to the whole production, namely fantasy is more real than reality. It furthers the whole difference between appearance and reality  that Chicago plays with to levels of inspired satire. We Both Reach for the Gun for example is closer to what the press conference is really about than what reality would show.  Furthermore, it makes the character of Roxie Hart much more comical, and satirical than she would be otherwise. Roxie Hart is a no talent hack; this is sorta the whole point of the thing; Roxie has to murder to get fame.  This is why, if judging from a purely music point of view, Zellweger sounds so bad. you see since Roxie is so deluded about her own talent level, and worth she believes that she is such a virtuoso that she doesnt think she needs to improve her voice, even in her fantasies.  This is why the song Roxie is so funny. which brings me to the direction, I wish Marshall has a long career in front of him because he really does a amazing job.  the imagery in all the songs, I particularly like the big shadow in Mr. Cellophane, the way he handles the actors, his framing and the way he use editing all add up to a film that shows, and not tells, is very layered (each song predicts the next one if you pay attention) and beyond clever (ladies and gentlemen a tap dance.) I still dont know how he managed to film Roxie with all the mirrors without the camera being shown. Also, Marshall understands that some times a single image is better, than a slew of clutter; something Lurhmann does not.  We both reach for the Gun is one of the best directional efforts I have every seen;  I cant tell you how much I love that scene.  that scene is definitely divinely inspired. 
 
 that is to say nothing of the film strongest element; its cast.  Renee Zellweger gives such a brave performance that I think she should have won, through Im not that upset about it.  Zellweger managed to sing bad enough to be to appear not talented, yet not so bad enough to be distracting and grating.  that is really amazing, and very brave as some people might actually call her a no talent hack, and mean it.  On top of that Zellweger managed to be as cute as a button, as sexy as a chorus dancer and a vindictive bitch, or whatever the scene required, with complete reality. She also managed to get Roxie empathy, without being likable, which itself is amazing.  Zeta-Jones lights up the screen in every dance number, and does what Zellweger does for Roxie with her Velma. (I totally agree with her win)  The two play off each with such force and timing that I cant decide who did a better job.  Richard Gere is the perfect, perfect Billy Flynn, and I dont mean that as a hyperbole. He should have been nominated, and I think that was his best performance ever. I know a lot of people have trouble with his singing, I dont obviously, but I really like his voice for Billy; it has this aged, slightly raspy quality to it, as if Billy has song the same songs too many times, which makes perfect sense, and fits like a glove.  Queen Latifah seems to have channeled Sophie Tucker (Ebert, I think, anyway I really agree).  Finally, Im sure Im the only person who thinks this on RT, but Reilly was the best supporting actor of 03.  His Amos is just right mixture of sap and common goodness and has all the best reaction shots (you are a disloyal husband.) in the film, and Reilly carries it very well.   I know a lot think Cooper in Adaptation, but I must confess I have no idea what the buzz is about for that performance. I wouldnt have nominated Cooper that year. (I would gladly listen to someone explain the buzz to me.)
 
 the production values speak for themselves; I so want Billys We Both Reached for the Gun suit.

This film is a mess. 
 
It's supposed to be the grand return of movie musical-dom. Instead, it is an ego trip masquerading as a film that is a task to finish watching. The 'plot' of said movie is that poor Ruby (Renne Zellweger) wants to be a star, and sees an opportunity to do it in the trial for shooting her husband John C. Reilly. Her lawywer Richard Gere believes he can get her off by staging publicity stunt after publicity stunt. Ruby's fellow inmate Catherine Zeta Jones, and warden Queen Latifah all have their own agendas. But all of them boil to wanting money/power and stopping at nothing to get it.
 
The film uses this skeletal plot, whose undergirding cynicism makes every action absurdly telegraphed, as a frame for hanging lots of the dance numbers on. These alternate between real and dream sequences. All of the stagings are confusing, the numbers uninteresting and forgettable, the coreography bland. 
 
Yet that is the not the thing that sinks this ship. Killing this entire endeavor and making it one of the most frustrating film experiences of 2002 is that "Chicago" is one of the worst edited films in history. The coverage is so poor you want to puke.
 
They do not hold a single shot for longer than four seconds. I counted! The frenzied cutting makes things confusing. In addition to that, the cuts are always to the wrong place. Some poor angle, some bizarre non sequitur; their choosing was haphazard. All the drama is edited into a pulp by a blizzard of cuts that slices up any mounting tension. The dance numbers are rendered useless. Instead of a long shot, medium width, of Catherine Zeta Jones dancing a number, we get a pastiche of close-ups and distance. The links between the various parts of her coreography are rendered invisible. We wonder if this all from the same take. Inconsistencies pop up. The patient desire to sink in and experience the number is replaced by the numbing number of new shots appearing from all different parts of the set, not because the story requires them, but because the filmmakers decided to throw in all they could. 
 
After thirty minutes of trying to observe the story through this haze, I decided I'd had enough and threw it into the lost cause camp. The rest of the time was spent nitpicking for things that were wrong and the list began to mount rapidly. All because the editor was on cocaine when he put it together and has no clue how to build a musical up. Stanley Holloway could not have stolen every scene in "My Fair Lady" had he been edited like this. One shudders to think how that movie would have turned out if done a la Chicago: A candy-colored survey of every possible angle of the pub while he belts out "With a Little Bit of Luck", all the while missing the most exciting part of the spectacle, his performance. 
 
Saving this mess from a one is purely Zeta Jones's obvious relish in performance. She wipes the floor with all of the participants, with only Gere not being totally upstaged. Her talent, energy, and skill are so evident they jump off the screen. Then again, she's so good she unbalances the entire picture by diverting our attention from the rest of the inferior cast. Who cares about John C. Reilly when Catherine Zeta Jones is vamping it up? But with that exception, I loathed this movie and shuddered when it inexplicably won "Best Picture".

Chicago is another solid musical in a time when respect for the genre is dying.  Instead of being upbeat and happy like many other, Chicago goes for a more cynical and dark humor feel that is satisfying and entertaining.  However, nothing in this movie screams best picture like the academy and all the buzz would have you believe.  Getting that out of the way -

The core of the story is the longing desire for popularity and the lengths people will go to achieve it.  After killing both her husband and sister (of course because her husband cheated on her for the sister), talented dancer and singer Velma Kelly was the most talked about person in town.  Was, until Roxie Hart kills the man she had an extra-marital affair with.  Suddenly, she is the spotlight.  Though, she begins to like the publicity and these two are in a struggle to receive more attention than the other.

The movie makes the good choice of making the promident perspective that of Roxie Hart.  In films using such dark humor, it can be easy to not care about a single character.  But Chicago is different.  It has a heart, at least for that of Roxie.  The other characters are morally corrupt, shallow people and Chicago in that respect, is never too deep with its cliched characters - not that one will mind a whole lot considering the cast.

A highly talented cast indeed, Chicago is a giant and even surprising crew at times.  Rene Zellwegger is the perfect choice for the naive Roxie.  However, Rene Zellwegger's talent of singing while solid, is not extraordinary and she sags slightly where all the other actors soar.  Richard Gere, Catherine Zeta Jones, John C. Reily, and Queen Latifah all exceed Rene Zellwegger to such an extent that it feels a little uneven.  

As stated earlier, Chicago is not so much a movie about substance than it is about style.  Anyone expecting an artistic achievement behind the screenplay will be dissapointed.  However, the zippy kill or be killed attitude with a delightfully sinful execution makes Chicago a cynical blast in a sense.  Characters lie, cheat, steal, murder, set one another up, but we love watching it the entire time.

The budget behind this block buster hit was surprisingly small.  In fact the budget was so conservative, most if not all of the movie was filmed in Canada because of the economic benefits of filming there.  Yet, you would never guess from its solid glossy sets, dirty streets, and lively dance clubs broght to life with liquor and jazz.

Chicago certainly is an entertaining musical, make no mistake of that.  It helps bring a genre long forgotten back into the light.  However, Chicago is not worthy of best picture, or even the nomination in my mind.  There were substantially better films that deserved nominations in directing, screen writting, and motion picture.  It simply was not the achievement that Moulin Rouge was.

A new interpretation that takes the award-winning Broadway show into fresh and expansive cinematic realms, Chicago shifts adroitly from the reality of intrigue, rivalry and betrayal to spectacular fantasies of music and dance, offering tongue-in-cheek commentary on the cult of celebrity and the scandalous lengths to which people will go to attain it.
 
I have never seen the original broadway show, and the movie was a first for me. I saw it after the Academy Awards crowned it 'Best Movie Of The Year'. I saw it after the mediatic fuss about how good it was. I saw it on DVD.
 
It's the movies' original ironic parable about criminals profiting from the celebrity of crime, with much more satiric relevance to today's media world than it had in earlier decades -- and the script plays this chord without hammering it to death, thank you. And though the musical is filled with big production numbers and chorus lines of dancers, first-time feature director Rob Marshall stages it with an air of minimalist intimacy and bathed in shadows. 
 
Budgeted at a modest $40 million, the movie has an even lower-budget look to it, with no big set pieces to evoke Jazz Age Chicago and an ingratiating awkwardness to the dance routines that make it seem more "Cabaret" than "Sweet Charity" in the canon of the musical's original choreographer, Bob Fosse. The biggest decision M. Marshall & Co. had to make -- staying traditional and resisting the impulse to turn the proceedings into an MTV-style musical -- definitely works: The old-fashioned material likely would disintegrate or at least lose much of its charm under the burden of light-paced cutting and zillions of camera angles. 
 
The movie-star casting also works. Zeta-Jones makes a wonderfully statuesque and bitchy saloon goddess; Gere exudes just the right bad-boy appeal as the opportunistic Irish lawyer; Zellweger is such a letter-perfect Roxie Hart that she is now one of my favorite actresses.
 
[b]Bottom Line : [/b]Competent, stylish, frequently funny, sexy, effective... and all that jazz!

Reilly's "Cellophane"  is particularly moving), and impressively executed by the actors themselves, the dancing as well as the singing. Roxie Hart (Renée Zellweger) watches Velma Kelly (Catherine Zeta-Jones) on a Chicago stage.  Just by looking at Roxie, we can see her desparation for stardom in her eyes while watching Velma sings her heart out.  As Velma reaches that showstopping note - "to do....that..." - Roxie, projecting herself onto the stage in her own mind, steals the note from her: "JAAAAAAAAAZZZZ!"  It's the first glimpse into Roxie's future and it's going to be one hell of a ride.
 
Director Rob Marshall's idea for presenting the musical numbers in [i]Chicago [/i]is simple, but effective.  He doesn't try and make us believe people are bursting into song and dance left and right, but he puts the songs in Roxie's imagination.  
 
The story in a nutshell: Roxie wants to be a star, she has an affair with her husband and then shoots her lover.  She then goes to jail, manipulates the press, and becomes the vaudeville star she's always wanted to be.

[size=2]Continuing with my look back at past Best Picture Winners are two more recent Oscar winners. 

The Academy Award Winner for Best Picture for 2001 went to [b]A Beautiful Mind[/b]. The other nominees for Best Picture included [i]Gosford Park[/i], [i]In the Bedroom[/i], [i]Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring[/i], and [i]Moulin Rouge[/i]. Other notable films include [i]Training Day,[/i] [i]Mulholland Dr.,[/i] [i]Memento[/i], [i]Monster's Ball[/i], [i]Iris[/i], [i]Shrek[/i], [i]Ghost World[/i], [i]The Royal Tenenbaums[/i], [i]Amelie[/i], and [i]Bridget Jones Diary[/i].

 

Directed by Ron Howard, [b]A Beautiful Mind[/b] is the story of John Nash, a brilliant [/size][font=Times New Roman][size=3]mathematician [/size][/font][size=2]and professor who also suffers from schizophrenia. Russell Crowe plays Nash, who we first see as a gruff, awkward and anti-social college student. He writes mathematical formulas on his dorm room window, doesn't fit in with the guys, and has no clue on who to approach women. Ron Howard (in a twist for him) doesn't immediatly reveal his mental illness, although it's not difficult for the viewer to realize there is something more going on with the unlikable, asocial Nash. A few years later, when Nash is well-known for his theories, he is recruited by CIA agent Parcher (Ed Harris) to help solve Soviet military codes. It doesn't take Einstein for the viewer to figure outt what's happening by now. Along the way Nash meets a beautiful student named Alicia (Jennifer Connelly) who soon becomes his wife. Soon afterwards Alicia realizes there is something more to Nash's bizarre behavior, and John winds up in a mental hospital. When he comes home he continues to act in a bizarre fashion. Eventually things get better (you knew they would) and all live happily ever after.

This film was a huge disappointment for me on so many levels. Ron Howard is one of Hollywood's most conventional directors. John Nash was anything but conventional. Howard's big twist was how he showed Nash's schizophrenia, but instead of being clever I found it halphhazard and irritating. Once he lets the viewers in on his secret (which I figured out long before Nash ended up in the hospital) it's nothing but pure formula for Howard. We need some tears and a happy ending, not a surprise, and that's what Howard delivers. I however wasn't buying! First off, Nash, now matter how you twist it, isn't a very likable character. Oh but he's schizophrenic you say! Sure that definitely had something to do with his personality, but most mentally ill people have some goodness in them that isn't completely alienated by the illness. Secondly, have we seen enough women like Alicia in movies? Love will conquer all? She was blindly supportive beyond reason. What brief bit of tension that was shown played about as well as Gangster rap at the Grand Ole Oprey. Lastly, this film just smirked "give me an Oscar" and by golly it got one! I don't hate Ron Howard as a director, but I despised this film despite a good performance by Russell Crowe. Goes down as one of the Worst Best Picture Winners in history in my opinion.

The Academy Award Winner for Best Picture for 2002 went to [b]Chicago[/b]. The other nominees for Best Picture were [i]Gangs of New York,[/i] [i]The Hours,[/i] [i]Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers[/i], and [i]The Pianist[/i]. Other notable films of 2002 include [i]Adaption[/i], [i]Catch Me If You Can[/i], [i]Road To Perdition[/i], [i]Far From Heaven,[/i] [i]Talk To Her[/i], and [i]About Schmidt.[/i] 

Directed by Rob Marshall, [b]Chicago [/b]is the screen adaption of the popular Broadway musical. Set in the 1920's, Roxie Hart (Renee Zellweger) is a young woman unhappily married to Amos (John C. Reilly) who desires to be a vaudeville star. Roxie idolizes Velma Kelly (Catherine Zeta-Jones) and is having an affair with a man named Fred Casley (Dominic West) that promises to make her as big a star as Velma. When he gets violent, Roxie shoots him. Initially Amos agrees to take the fall until he finds out Roxie was having an affair. Once in prison, Roxie is surprised to find that Velma is also there. Both hook up with superstar lawyer Billy Flynn (Richard Gere) who has never lost a case. Flynn's strategy is to create a media circus behind each case, garnering public support for his defendants. At the same time Roxie and Velma compete for Flynn's attention, and most importantly the limelight in this media circus.

Simply said, [b]Chicago[/b] is a delight. Where most musicals fail to transfer successfully to the big screen, [i]Chicago [/i]strikes a perfect balance with a compelling enough story for the big screen and well placed and performed musical numbers. Catherine Zeta-Jones looks like she belongs on the stage, she's a great dancer and has a wonderful voice. Renee Zellweger is alternately sweet and sassy, always a delight watch. Richard Gere, Queen Latifah and John C. Reilly are also very good. Never a dull moment in this quickly paced film. Although I loved [i]The Pianist[/i], I have no complaints with this Best Picture Winner. [i]

[font=Courier New]Ive always had an odd fascination with musicals. There comes a point in your life for movie lovers when you see a movie that changes everything you think you know about movies. When I first saw Frank Ozs [i]Little Shop of Horrors[/i], I was taken back at what I was seeing. Before that moment, I had never seen a movie where non-animated characters were singing. And I had never seen a movie where most of the scenes looked like stage sets. But something clicked in me, and this film worked. Sure it isnt on my Top Ten, but that doesnt change the fact that it opened my eyes to Live Action Musicals. 

Its rare for me to have a favorite movie of the year that is actually nominated for Best Picture at the Academy Awards. And its even rarer for me to have a favorite movie of the year that actually wins Best Picture. [i]Chicago[/i] is one of those rare moments. [i]Chicago[/i] is a movie that is so slick, so marvelous, so flashy and beautiful that it is hard to find any real fault with it. I usually set a minimum of five years after I first see the movie before it is considered a Great Film, but what is a couple of months short of that?

After seeing Chris Columbus film version of [i]Rent[/i], I was reminded of Rob Marshalls adaptation of [i]Chicago[/i]. Like [i]Rent[/i], Ive never seen [i]Chicago[/i] performed live. I expect that the show is better than the movie, which is usually the case. But the film version of this story is still an impressive piece of work. The fact that the seemingly impossible task of turning this show into a movie produced one of the best films in the past 5 years is a monumental achievement. 

The first time I heard about [i]Chicago[/i] was during an interview Rosie ODonnell was having with Madonna. Both were fans of the show, and expressed interest in a film version. I also heard that Nathan lane was interested. Now, I dont have any real problems with any of these people. I still admire Madonnas music, and have found a few films of Lane and ODonnell to be entertaining. But I doubt that these three could have pulled off the same classy movie we have now.

Its amazing to see that some of the actors in this film had no previous music experience before this film. This would appear to be a problem, since most musicals try to cast actors who have already proved they can sing and dance. But Richard Gere and Renee Zellweger prove they are such diverse actors, that this movie isnt that hard for them to shine in.

Catherine Zeta-Jones, who has had experience in singing and dancing, is the real star of the movie though. Her performance of Velma Kelly, who has murdered her husband and sister after catching them spread eagle, is a incredible performance, and well deserving of the Oscar she received for it. And who can forget Queen Latifah as Matron Mama Morton, warden of the prison our two main characters are in. She comes on strong, and reminds us that she was once and always a great singer. 

John C. Reilly portrays the ever faithful husband to Zellwegers Roxie, Amos Hart. Ive loved Reilly in almost everything I have seen him. My first experience was in [i]Boogie Nights[/i], and then when he worked with director Paul Thomas Anderson in [i]Magnolia[/i] (a future entry in the Great Films list). He may not have the average look of a real star, but his talent proves otherwise. 

This was Rob Marshalls debut film. A veteran of the stage, I can see why someone as talented as Marshall would be picked for this sort of film. Recently he directed the critically panned [i]Memoirs of a Geisha[/i], and I kind of have the feeling that Chicago might be his only real success. You never know though. But even if it turns out that way, will it be that bad to be remembered only for a film like this?

Musicals dont seem to work with audiences today, that is why it is risky to make them. I guess people still have a hard time believing a movie where people break into song. But this movie does something different. Sure they are singing, but not the traditional way musicals have done in the past. The songs are done as stage performances, and are presented more as a way to better express the emotions in the film. They are lively, colorful and simply dazzling! One of the best soundtracks I have ever heard!

When I first saw the film in theaters, I was blown away. Owning it on DVD, I find myself yearning to experience this movie once again on the big screen. There was just something about the film that worked so well in the theater with a large audience. Nevertheless, I highly recommend this movie to anyone who hasnt seen it before, and even though who have should see it again. Musicals are a difficult style of film to pull together these days, but [i]Chicago[/i] proves it still can be done. [/font]

Not a huge fan of director Rob Marshall, but him directing this movie Chicago shows that he has talent. This movie Chicago is based on the hit Broadway show and it's about two woman named Velma Kelly and Roxie Hart and they find themselves on death row together and they both fight for the fame that will keep them from the gallows in 1920s Chicago. Catherine Zeta-Jones and Renee Zellweger play the two leads, Richard Gere co-stars as there lawyer, Queen Latifah plays a prison guard named Mama Morton and John C. Reilly plays Roxie's husband Amos. As for all these actors in this movie they all play pretty good roles, I really didn't find John C. Reilly very good in this because he usually does Comedy movies and I honestly I think he should stick to that. Now as for Richard Gere he was a little better than John C. Reilly, his acting was really good but his singing not so much. Renee Zellweger and Queen Latifah were really good in this movie, they both got into there roles very well and they both have very talented singing voices. But now we get to Catherine Zeta-Jones, she was phenomenal in this movie, seriously. Almost every scene she was in she dominated, her singing in this movie was powerful, her dancing was really sexy and her performance was top notch, you can really see why she won the Academy Award. Anyways I should talk about the actual movie. This movie Chicago is not my favorite Musical but it sure is a good one. Chicago brings everything you want in a musical, it has great songs, great dancing and a very good cast. Like I said I don't care for Rob Marshall very much, but he directed this movie very well, the camera shots worked really good, the stage setting was perfect and the movie was really clear on it's story. So if you haven't seen this movie yet I would check it out, I know some guys will not like this movie because it's not an Action movie, but I say give this movie a chance because you might enjoy it.

From its opening note to its final beat, Chicago presents a razzle-dazzle spectacle of song and dance that will make your head spin with its kaleidoscope of cynicism, wit and flash. Mix that with surprisingly adept turns from a group of performers not known for their singing and dancing skills and you have the makings of a noisy, colorful rat-a-tat-tat extravaganza.

The most delightful aspect of Chicago is watching stars Renee Zellweger, Catherine Zeta-Jones and Richard Gere display talents few of us knew they had. The trio, along with Queen Latifah and John C. Reilly, perform their own singing and dancing. And they are all surprisingly really really really good.

The musical's glitz comes with a sharp edge, a satirical study of celebrity and the lengths some people will go to achieve it. Velma Kelly (Zeta-Jones) is Chicago's most famous vaudeville star and Roxie Hart (Zellweger) wants to emulate her. Their paths cross in the city's women prison where Velma is incarcerated for killing her husband and sister, while Roxie is charged with shooting her lover.
With the help of crooked matron Mother Morton (Queen Latifah), Roxie meets and hires legendary lawyer Billy Flynn (Gere) to represent her. Flynn, who has never lost a case, also represents Velma. And when he switches his attentions to Roxie, a bitter rivalry ensues between the star and would-be diva, each playing a game of one-upmanship to retain Flynn's representation.

A movie musical is a tricky beast because the filmmakers work to adhere to some unwritten cinematic rules of reality, as they inject music and dance - not something people do everyday in real life. Director-choreographer Rob Marshall and screenwriter Bill Condon solve that dilemma by showing most of the musical numbers through Roxie's eyes. They are merely figments of her overactive imagination.
This device allows for some clever and stylish numbers, ranging from a prison-block tango to Queen Latifah's hot and sexy chanteuse number, "When You're Good to Mama."
Marshall and Condon's tack works wonders as it allows them free rein to create a variety of snappy set pieces, ranging from Gere's manipulating the press like a puppet master during "The Press Conference Rag," to Reilly's sad-clown rendition of "Mr. Cellophane."
One number has Zellweger's Roxie extolling her husband's virtues for taking the rap for the killing she committed, then in mid-song switching to a vitriolic lament about what a loser he was after he recanted because he discovered Roxie cheated on him.

The performances are outstanding. Zeta-Jones is brassy and conniving as Velma, while Zellweger's Roxie hides her ambitious exterior behind a baby-doll look of innocence. Gere is sharp and light on his feet as the quick-thinking lawyer. Queen Latifah is wonderfully droll as Mother Morton, while the solid and versatile Reilly adds to his growing credits of character roles. The film's main characters are despicable, but the movie is so much fun that you find yourself rooting for some of Broadway's shadiest characters. 
By the time it ends in a rush of sequins, flashbulbs, and back-stabbing babes, it has said plenty about how show business has infiltrated every corner of society. A glitzy, seductive, high-energy movie that isn't just the most explosively entertaining musical in a couple of decades. It's going to be the most influential.

Brassy and entertaining, but sort of an empty delight at the end of it all. I immensely admire the technical wizardry and actorly flair that oozes from Chicago but musicals are really just not my thing. And I dunno, the 20s flapper era strikes me as so simple. I think to an interested party, this would be the absolute Holy Grail, as the whole affair is arguably faultless within its own little warped world (except Richard Gere, he sucks so bad, make him go awayyyy). I would be remiss to deny that I liked the movie - of course I did. Renee Zellweger falling down and awkwardly declaring a pregnancy, and Catherine Zeta-Jones' reaction, were movie magic. 

The music is accessible and well-done; Cell Block Tango is stunning, CZJ is solid gold, and you can't help but fall in love with Queen Latifah after Be Good to Mama. And seriously, who the hell would have expected that voice coming out of John C. Reilly? Amazing. Everything about this movie, right down to the costume and set design, is crafted with utmost cinematic love. Rob Marshall has created a beautiful paean to an art form that clearly means the world to him. I won't seek fault in it to justify my personal feelings, but simply admit that it isn't a movie for me.

A few years ago, "Chicago" had a nice showing at the Oscars, taking home six trophies including Best Picture.  Since then, it's gotten a lot of flack for not being as good as it was said to be.  I've read numerous times how it was a mistake to give it so many honors, but watching it, I really don't feel that way.  Is it a better movie than "Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers"?  Nah, but I don't mind that it won at all.  It's a great movie, and (along with "Moulin Rouge!"), it has helped usher in the new wave of movie musicals that now continues with "Phantom," "Rent," and this year's "Hairspray," "Across the Universe," and "Sweeney Todd."
 
There are a few things that really set "Chicago" apart from other musicals.  One of the most notable is the plot, which isn't the simplistic romantic stuff that many musicals present using different time periods and such.  Instead, we're treated to the story of Roxie Hart (Renee Zellweger)-an aspiring dancer who murders her lying lover and ends up in jail, where she teams up with lawyer Billy Flynn (Richard Gere), who has never lost a case.  She feels she has nothing to worry about, as she's a woman, but Chicago in the 1920s is changing, and when another woman is hanged, Roxie realizes how serious her ordeal is.
 
It's not the typical story that's used in a musical, but that's what makes it so refreshing, and I think it probably has something to do with how successful it was, too.  Some of the songs (particularly "Cell Block Tango") share the same darker tone and help to make the movie serious, something a lot of musicals can't quite manage to do (the reason most are musical comedies, yeah?).
 
The cast is fantastic.  Four of the main five were nominated for Oscars, and all were well deserving.  I'm really surprised Gere was overlooked, though, as his performance was probably my favorite of all.  His singing was a little weak, I suppose (I noticed this particularly in "Razzle Dazzle"), but he's still perfect in the part.  Catherine Zeta-Jones is also amazing in her part, especially in her big dance number, "I Can't Do It Alone."  I almost get out of breath just watching it.
 
The main thing that differentiates "Chicago" is the manner in which the musical numbers play into the movie.  Instead of the characters just bursting into song (this happens a few times, but only when it makes sense), the songs are musical representations of what's happening in the story.  For instance, during the movie's best number, "We Both Reached For the Gun," Billy Flynn uses Roxie as a ventriloquist dummy while a bunch of marionette reporters are manipulated by his choice words.  It's one of the most creative numbers I've seen in any musical.  Another example is Billy's tap dance, which happens while he's engaging in a moment of high tension in the courtroom-it's good stuff.

I'll admit I didn't like it immediately, the first hour drawing a few yawns. However the brilliance of this movie gradually began to unfold. The vaudeville acts were suddenly captivating, seamlessly integrating with a plot suddenly as unforgiving as Memento. Sharp sympathy blends with a desire for justice as the luck of Velma and Roxie rises and falls, leading you from satisfaction to disappointment, pinpointing the unrelenting and dirty atmosphere of the 1920?s, Jazz age Chicago. However, all my credit must fall to the astounding dedication and brilliance of ALL the actors. As if they were born into their roles (possibly even better than in LOTR), Catherine Zeta-Jones and Renée Zellweger (in particular) display amazing talent (every aspect of Velma and Roxie including, surprisingly, the singing were performed by their respective actors) and passion in their roles. Chicago is a hugely entertaining film which subtly displays shades of seriousness, and is definitely worthy of its praise and awards, if only because of its brilliant and captivating characters.

A fantastic musical that brings the rousing communal experience of watching live theater into a dark, popcorn-scented movie theater. The songs are very catchy and the dance numbers will likely prompt you to stand and dance along (or in my case, stealthily tap my toes on the floor). Catherine Zeta-Zones as Velma literally vamps it up and usually steals the show when she's around with Renee Zellwegger. The number "I Can't Do It Alone" is exhaustingly fun and this is where Zeta-Jones really shines. You wished you could just put on your dancing shoes and join her. Zellwegger, who plays Roxie Hart, is a surprise nonetheless. Her number "Roxie" evokes a Marilyn Monroesque sensuality: buxom, playful and sexual. The last number, "Nowadays/Hot Honey Rag Medley Title" is explosive, as it literally showcases the two dancing women against a backdrop of a giant and blindingly flashing billboard. Fun, flashy and trampy just like the two leading ladies, "Chicago" is pure, unadulterated fun. My only qualm is that the set pieces are a little limited and narrow, and Marshall shoots the scenes, as if he really is viewing at a live stage. Film is a different medium, and a widespan scan could have made the musical numbers more grandiose. Nevertheless, this is only a minor detail. One of the best musicals ever made: That's "Chicago".

Rob Marshall's Chicago is full of electrifying song and dance numbers, great performances and many themes that ing true to the early 20th century. The costumes look stunning, the choreography is wonderful and who knew Richard Gere and John C Reilly could sing. The movie struggles to keep up the excitement for much of the movie, and the story isn't too involving, but there is too much symbolism, energy and thoughtfulness to not call Chicago one of the better musicals of this millennium. The musical number all represent the actions and thoughts of the characters which i thought was ingenious. There is also the issue of a lust for fame and how it can blind you from what people really think. I liked all of the performances, and some of the dance numbers were very inventive and smart. Basically when your in Chicago, you need to get famous or else you will get nowhere, and in this case, you must be famous to get out of jail. While the movie burst onto the screen with intense opening numbers, the movie is very slow and downcast with its tone for the rest of the movie. I wish it had kept the electricity for much more of the film and i would have enjoyed it more. Still, this is an incredibly visionary and smart musical, and dare i say I am actually interested to see what Rob Marshall can do next with his new movie Nine coming out in December with Daniel Day Lewis. Chicago is not for everyone, but the power and symbolism of the singing and dancing is going to pull you into the thick of it. Thumbs up!

Both musicals and movies are notorious as ineffective vehicles of artistic expression, so there seems to be little hope for the movie musical. Then came along this movie, which completely reinvented the genre. How amazing that a 1970s musical based on a 1920s play can carry such a relevant and important message to our society! This film speaks volumes about celebrity, the insincerity of our culture, and the flaws of human nature. Rob Marshall handled the transition to film exceedingly well, asking us not to suspend our disbelief when the characters begin to sing but putting the musical sequences in a heightened fantasy world that stands in stark contrast to the plot at hand and actually elevates the story instead of getting in the way. And, of course, both the dramatic and musical performances are top-notch.

Musicals are made (or unmade) by their songs and actors, and Chicago excels in one of these categories while being a little more questionable in the other. 

It's no exaggeration to say that some of these song numbers are among the most famous and well-known musical performances, ever. Cell Block Tango, We Both Reached for the Gun, And All That Jazz...you don't have to be a huge theater fan to recognize these favorites. And even if this is your first exposure to them, expect to have them running through your mind days after you hear them. A few of the songs pale in comparison to the most popular ones, but overall the tunes in Chicago can stand toe-to-toe with nearly any other musical.

The big turn-off for me was the casting. Renee Zellweger simply failed to bring the character of Roxie to life, I don't know how else to put it. I didn't enjoy her character at all. Catherine Zeta-Jones, Queen Latifah and Richard Gere are more suited to their roles, but they still aren't as good as one could have wished. Lucy Liu was awesome in her brief part, though. 

Anyway, Chicago is a good enough movie musical, but when the main character is ineptly handled it makes the whole experience less enjoyable for me. I'd rather just hear the songs and skip past Renee's weird faces and unconvincing acting.

Once upon a time, long ago, a musical movie would open and go on to become the top-grossing movie of the year. Sometimes they even cleaned up at the Academy Awards, too. Since the 1970's, however, the number of musicals that have been given the big screen treatment is slim. You've got Evita with Madonna, Little Shop of Horrors from 1986, and I guess a few animated films could fit into this category too. In recent years, more often than not, studios will only greenlight a musical if it's got "independent release" written all over it (think Hedwig and the Angry Inch, Dancer in the Dark, and, before it exploded in popularity, 2001's Moulin Rouge!). Now, thanks to proper promotion, critical praise, and healthy production values, the newest entry in the category could really spark a return to form for the once-glorious genre. It's the highly-anticipated Chicago, an adaptation of the saucy 1975 Broadway hit that put the expression "All That Jazz" on the map. 

This incarnation stars Renée Zellweger as Roxie Hart, a whimsical wife who shoots her blasé lover after he tells it like it is. With little help from her relatively slow husband Amos (John C. Reilly), she ends up getting sent to prison. So too does Velma Kelly (Catherine Zeta-Jones), a dancer whom Roxie has admired. Velma has killed her husband and her sister when she caught them fooling around and is now awaiting trial. The big-busted "Mama" Morton (played with show-stopping vigour by Queen Latifah) suggests recruiting Billy Flynn (Richard Gere), who has purportedly never lost a case. As the media scrums turn the murders into front page fodder (sound familiar?), Roxie begins to enjoy her newfound celebrity. 

The film marks yet another collaboration from the songwriting team of John Kander and Fred Ebb, who have had one of the greatest and longest-running music-and-lyrics relationships in theatre history (Cabaret, Steel Pier, Kiss of the Spider-Woman). They are rarely hesitant to accentuate the sensuality of their characters, and Chicago is no exception. Some numbers boast chorus lines of women in black lingerie, while others have dance steps that might make even Bob Fosse (the choreographer) himself blush. But although the subject matter frequently gravitates towards sensual themes, the musical itself is not overtly sexy. It is energetically always moving forwards, propelling the satirical narrative, and not caring to stop for incidental teases along the way. 

Directed by veteran Broadway director Rob Marshall, Chicago has an impressive array of songs that are catchy and, more importantly, actually work with the story and not against it. "Cell Block Tango" ("He Had It Coming"), "Razzle Dazzle", "Roxie", and "Mister Cellophane" are all excellent character pieces (for Velma, Billy, Roxie, and Amos respectively). The real standouts are Latifah's "When You're Good To Mama", and "We Both Reached for the Gun", which is set against a series of marionettes that is as eerie as it is inspired. Incidentally, watch for the Spider-Woman herself, Chita Rivera, in a brief cameo. 

Clearly, one of the predominant questions will be whether Chicago is as good a movie as Moulin Rouge!, which was nominated for best picture last year. Personally, since I was not a fan of the 2001 smash hit, the choice is obvious. Marshall's film is in a class all its own. However, since I am apparently in a minority in regards to the merits of Moulin, its likeability by others will probably be determined by other factors, such as whether or not one is looking to hear previously released music, or if one prefers songs that have been written specifically for the material. Another factor will be the performances, which in my esteem are quite accomplished here, but I could probably understand if someone were to take a contrary position on this point. 

It has come to my attention that the floodgates have now officially opened thanks to films like Chicago. Several Broadway musicals are scheduled to finally be adapted into film, and I for one am ecstatic. It's my understanding that Joel Schumacher's Phantom of the Opera is now in post-production, and an adaptation of the late Jonathan Larson's influential breakthrough Rent is scheduled for a 2004 release. The prospects are encouraging, and it's a great time to be a fan of Broadway musicals.

Seriously, what else could you want in a musical? There are those who, even to this day, like to rip on Chicago because there isn't a likeable character among the bunch. Fine--wallow in Sandra Bullock goo.

Chicago is based on Bob Fosse's Broadway smash, and onscreen it razzles and it dazzles! Though it's set in 1920's Chicago, it's story of two ladies, Roxie Hart (Renee Zellweger) and Velma Kelly (a fabulously pregnant Catherine Zeta-Jones) both went for the gun when they were done wrong by the men in their lives. But both get help from smooth-talking lawyer Billy Flynn (Richard Gere) so they can get out of the prison run by Matron Mama Thornton (Queen Latifah, delightful) and they plan to get the tabloids on their side. How much has changed since those days?

Director Rob Marshall, a Broadway vet himself with television credits made a debut that single-handedly revitalized the movie musical. Together with screenwriter Bill Condon, they deliver a take-no-prisoners, hard-assed script that re-imagines the musical numbers for an audience raised on MTV. It's no wonder Chicago took nearly all of the top honors at that year's Academy Awards, including Best Picture.

As for the cast? Well Zellweger and Zeta-Jones bring the house dowm, tearing into classic numbers from John Kander and Fred Ebb (also responsible for the songs from my favorite film Cabaret) and they both dance with wild abandon (especially Zeta-Jones, who took the Best Supporting Actress Oscar). Zeta-Jones, looking like a Y2K Cyd Charisse steals the show with her pitch-perfect rendition of 'All That Jazz'. It's hot, hot hot! Gere, normally pretty low-key and laid back, has never been more vibrant and jubilant in a movie. To see him tap his way through the court is one for the time capsule. Zellweger has never been better onscreen either, even when abusing her goody-good husband, Amos (John C. Reilly-who does a great 'Mr. Cellophane').

Then there's that prison number, which pops like nothing else onscreen. Chicago is a musical and cinematic delight from start to finish, and must also be credited with bringing show-tune camp back to the mainstream (have you seen Glee lately?). It's wild, it's near-depraved, it's dazzling! It's dynamite!

Chicago is the film adaptation of the Broadway hit musical, based on the book written by Maurine Dallas Watkins. (Now that was a mouthful.)

The film version stars Renee Zellweger and Catherine Zeta-Jones as fame seeking femme-fatales, both in jail and under trial for murder. Richard Gere plays their slick attorney trying to get them both out of jail.

The film uses most of the songs from the Broadway musical. My personal favorite of the music numbers is Queen Latifah singing "When You're Good to Mama" as the prison warden, while flashing back and forth between the prison and her singing the song in a 1920's speak easy.

The movie is extremely well done from start to finish and reminds me a lot of work by the director Baz Luhrmann. It is obvious that the film's budget was spent on the lavish sets and costumes.

The acting is top rate and every character in the film is believable. Even Richard Gere pulls off his performance as the lawyer well, which was quite a surprise. Who knew that he could tap-dance?

The first time I saw Chicago, I only gave it a low seven because its story wasn't that great; it's a prison movie, who would've thought? Watching it again and knowing what exactly was going to say, I'm happy to admit it improved; instead of caring about the story, I focused on the visual treat that the film really is, and now I award it a marginal eight.

Probably why Chicago won the Academy's heart (when films like The Pianist, Gangs of New York and Adaptation were more deserving) was it has a big bang of an ending, great musical numbers and solid acting. It's a good thing that all the great, raunchy jazzeriffic tunes distract, because the film's storyline, like I said before, is a bit weak. And the songs may be a bit long, but the songs! They are great! Zellwegger, Zeta-Jones, Latifah and Reilly were all spectacular, on and off the stage. I don't usually like Richard Gere, and he was the weakest link, but still much better than usual. The great cast, flawless dancing and pitch-perfect singing were great.

Any and all overwhelming praise for Chicago would go to Bill Condon, the director. Not only are the songs very well coreographed, but the theatrical lighting make them all the more dynamic. Actually, the more I think about it, Chicago is a just plain wierd film, and Condon did a good job making it easy to understand.  It's fun, it's energetic, and it's easily accessible. I could see me watching it a third time in the near future; for all its flaws and all (but one, Best Supporting Actress) of its undeserved Oscars, it's a pretty darn good musical. And it was filmed in Canada!

"With the right song and dance, you can get away with murder." Murderesses Velma Kelly (a chanteuse and tease who killed her husband and sister after finding them in bed together)and Roxie Hart (Who killed her boyfriend when she discovered he wasn't going to make her a star) find themselves on death row together and fight for the fame that will keep them from the gallows in 1920s Chicago. REVIEW This movie is brilliantly acted and wonderfully directed. Catherine Zeta-Jones superb portrayal of saucy Velma Kelly is matched against Renee Zellweger's equally manipulative Roxie Hart. Neither of these characters is worth redeeming, but the audience will root for them anyway. Set in Prohibition Chicago, where jazz clubs are sheik and murder is a form of entertainment, Roxie Hart (Zellweger) is on trial for her life. Enter Billy Flynn (Richard Gere) a flamboyant lawyer more interested in manipulating the press than whether his client is guilty or innocent. Also features Queen Latifah as the warden who takes care of her charges...for a price! The musical sequences are very well done, most notably "Press Room Rag" and of course the signature "All that Jazz". Also, kudos to John C. Reilly whose "Mr. Cellophane" solo is heartbreaking poignant.

Musically rich but morally bankrupt, this jazzy romp follows Roxie Hart, a young woman who dreams of being a singer but ends up on Chicago's Muderess Row after killing her no-good lover.  There, she meets and locks horns with fellow chanteuse Velma Kelly, as they compete for Billy Flynn, the slickest, sleaziest defense lawyer in Chicago.  Their battle is bitchy and nasty, but like watching a train wreck, you can't look away, even when the few characters that aren't total assholes all suffer tragic fates.  Luckily, that isn't too painful, because the movie cares more about entertaining you with its "razzle-dazzle" jazz numbers than pulling you into the story.

The movie is a dazzling song and dance extravaganza, with just enough words to support the music and allow everyone to catch their breath between songs. [b][color=black]Like I have said before, musicals have to be VERY good for me like them, and [i]Chicago[/i] is definetly one of the better musicals that I have seen. The cast is pretty amazing, I've always loved Queen Latifah and Richard Gere, both of whom had strong performances in this one. Gere pulls off his usual charm and is pretty funny at some points too! However this is the first movie I've seen from Zellweger and Zeta-Jones. Zellweger seems to be a pretty decent actress with just some natural funniness to her. Zeta-Jones on the other hand seems to have the superior musical talent in this one and her acting is very good as well.[/color][/b]

[b][color=#000000]The story of [i]Chicago[/i] is pretty funny but dark as well. Most of the humor comes from women getting away with murder thanks to Gere as their lawyer and then Chicago glorifies the women and they become "celebrities" for 15 min of fame. Dark humor I guess you could say...but I think it's better than the usual "love love love" stories that come along with musicals.[/color][/b]

[b][color=#000000]The music itself is pretty catchy and overall very good. It's all done very well and just keeps you watching. The songs were upbeat and just felt like they were off of Broadway. Again, my favorite was Zeta-Jones. Whenever she was onscreen performing, you can't take your eyes of her...she has one of the greatest screen presences I have seen in a while. [/color][/b]

[b][color=#000000]The feel of this movie was just very good...the music was great, the costumes were great, the cast was great, and the story was great too...not much more you can ask for with a musical like this. This isn't the typical kind of musical so even if you don't really care for them you might enjoy this like I did. And if you love musicals, you are sure to love this one! Check it out![/color][/b]

A musical for people who think choreography happens in the editing suite, "Chicago" happily murders all that was exciting and biting in the original stage show and buries the corpse under a mountain of glitz.  Focus was shifted from dark look at the desperate greed that fuels the American Way of Life to ho-hum satire on the sitting duck of celebrity culture (interesting that they should have cut off the poisoned final words of the farewell from the movie version...) and dramatic balance was destroyed by filtering the whole piece through Roxie Hart's consciousness, thus making her counterpart Velma Kelly into a supporting act, so that the whole thing became RenÃ©e Zellweger's vehicle (and she plays Roxie as a better coordinated Bridget Jones in flapper costume), thus adding an extra layer of sanitisation (and robbing us of one of the best songs in the score, "Class", which in the show happens outside Roxie's frame of reference).  In short, everything that made "Chicago" a worthy successor to "Cabaret" was shoved to a side.  Not happy with this butchery, Rob Marshall treated the dance numbers as MTV fodder, chop chop chopping away so that one has no sense whatsoever of the space the dancers inhabit or how their bodies evolve within it (both surely essential elements to any choreography).  This whole enterprise is execrable, but two moments escape the butchery: the inventive (and excellent) staging of "We both reached for the gun" and Queen Latifah's jaw-dropping rendition of "When you're good to mama".  It is because of these two numbers that I am giving the whole one star - but since this is a big videoclip trying to pass for a musical anyway, maybe it would be better to just keep the two songs and burn the rest.

There is a lot wrong with it, but also a lot of good.  I really enjoyed some of the dance numbers, the way that it was shot like it was on a stage, how the ending is shot more like a film than the rest of it, and the satire that's built on the media.  But the story line seemed weak.  Supposedly, it's supposed to be about two women who are fighting over the spotlight and want to become legends.  This is mentioned for Roxie's character, but Velma is hardly spoken of.  I felt like Velma was underused.  We start out the movie with she and Roxie equally, yet we only get a small dose of Velma throughout the rest of the film.  Momma was hardly used as well, which would have been fine if she didn't have such a large entrance into the movie.  And the story line doesn't really match up.  Billy Flynn starts up with Velma, then Roxie comes along (not really spoken of by the media), and he says he will take care of her for $5,000.  He actually does it for much less and for really no reason whatsoever.  He makes Roxie a star.  Why didn't he do that for any of the other women in there?  In the end, Velma is out of prison and wants to tour with Roxie since she needs her in the act.  How did Velma get out so quickly when her court date kept getting pushed back?  There were a lot of things I didn't buy with the story.  To me, it was very poorly written, but beautifully shot and had some good ideas, but had great performances by Catherine Zeta-Jones and Richard Gere.  Renee Zellweger had her moments, but some scenes just made me cringe (like when she kills her lover).  The dark story line and humor is pretty much what got me through Chicago.  I'd give this one a 2.5/5.

It took a couple times for me to really love Chiago, since the first few I was comparing the movie to the live show I'd seen a few years earlier.  As one who loves musicals on film and on stage, I've learned that film musicals are often a lot different.  Songs get cut out or shortened, certain aspects of the script or plot might get changed around a bit.  But after my initial shock of "omg why did they cut out this song, or do this" I found myself really enjoying Chicago.  The style of the movie, exploring the seedy underworld of Chicago's jazz and liquor lifestyle stayed constant and up to par with the stage show.  Catherine Zeta-Jones is fantastic as Velma Kelly, a nightclub act who goes to jail for shooting her sister and husband.  Renee Zellweger (who I usually  don't enjoy) actually gave a really good performance as Roxie Hart, the sweet newcomer to the Chicago murder circuit.  And Richard Gere (although his singing was a bit nasaly for me, but was otherwise fine) gives a great performance as sleazy lawyer Billy Flynn.  Queen Latifah's role was small, but she steals every scene she's in as Mama Morton.  The rest of the cast did a wonderful job as well.  In my opinion I simultaneously loved and disliked the big show numbers for Chicago.  On one hand it helps the movie stay accurate to the stage version, literally translating the songs in a similar from stage to film.  But in another way it doesn't bring anything new to the film and reminds the audience (or at least it did with me) that this is just a razzle dazzle musical.  Still if you can just go along with what you're watching, you'll probably find Chicago to be an enjoyable, dark and fun film.
