Chicago offers some of the silver screen's best available musical cinema, because it's a complex tale of crime set in the 1920's Chicago which uses flashy glamourous musical numbers to make it a powerful visual experience too. Director Rob Marshall pieces Chicago together very well, building on the cleverly satirical story of the original play and piecing in a fine visual style composed of Academy Award worthy production design and costumes as well as the technical achievement of excellent cinematography and editing. That gives Chicago the strong visual style it needs, but Rob Marshall refuses to stop there. He gives it literally everything he has, and builds the style of the film up bigger and bigger until it explodes as a glamorous paradigm of musical cinema and utter entertainment, as well as being a cleverly satirical piece about fame which moves its usual story into a complex and fresh context packed to the brim with creativity. Thanks to Rob Marshall's direction, Chicago is a lot of things: its extremely clever, its humourous, its entertaining, its sexy and its visually creative. One thing it is definitely not is boring.
Chicago is a powerful addition to the credibility of many genres, and one of them is definitely musical cinema because due to the excellently written musical numbers which are choreographed with grace and gusto and are sung with a true firery passion which is what makes it the incredible splendour it needs to be as a means of succeeding as well as standing out. Chicago is a fine musical and a great film in general, and frankly its my favourite live action musical film second only to The Rocky Horror Picture Show.
See, it's the cast which renders Chicago such a diversely successful film because it has some of the most talented and sexy male and female actors available today put on board, and they rock the boat and raise the roof for viewers to a significant satisfaction.
Renee Zellwegger gives one of the greatest performances of her career as the lead in Chicago. Her absolute spirited stage charisma is all too powerful, and her manipulation of words and the minds of the surrounding characters makes her all too easy to sympathise with. Her amiable charm is all too rich for the screen, and she is absolutely perfect in Chicago because she uses all her charm as an actress and elements of sex appeal to make her a powerful character. Her performance is clear Oscar nomination material.
Richard Gere also gives Chicago some of his finest work, achieving the perfect soul of both a vaudevillian and a lawyer at the same tine in his performance and imploring the perfectly swift and confident line delivery necessary to characterise Billy Flynn perfectly. Richard Gere proves his stage skills in Chicago, and its unmissable for any of his fans.
Catherine Zeta-Jones undoubtedly achieves the best performance of her career in Chicago. Not only is she extremely powerful in her line delivery and her emotional strength within her facial gestures is rich, but she is incredibly sexy. Catherine Zeta-Jones makes the source of her sex appeal not in her body, but the way she uses it. The way she bends and flexes her body in several directions for the artistic merit of the dance choreography in Chicago is powerful, and her grittily strong and determined line delivery matched with her incredible singing voice makes her performance a sexy and emotional extravaganza which scored her the 2002 Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress deservingly.

There are far more interesting aspects at work here, including themes about media culture, infidelity, and the legal system. But yes, the songs are good too.

Chicago stars Renée Zellweger (Tom Cruise's weepy girlfriend from Jerry MaGuire) as Roxie, a woman who cheats on her husband, then kills the man she's sleeping with and gets sent to prison. She soon figures out that the only way to survive is to gain media attention and become a sort of a criminal pop star. Her ploy works, with newspapers churning out tabloid drivel about her, reporters lining up to talk to her, and men across the country obsessing over her. She's helped along in her exploits by her lawyer (Richard Gere), who manipulates the press and performs dance numbers in his underwear, a fellow inmate (Catherine Zeta-Jones), and her woman's prison's tough warden (Queen Latifah). 

Okay, this movie isn't for everyone. In fact, it's not really even for me. But what I enjoyed about it was its undeniable approachability. This movie doesn't go out of its way to try and imitate actual Broadway productions of the play it's based off of. Rather, it attempts to take the stage format and inject some life into it by putting it on the silver screen. And it works well up to a certain point-- sure, you end up wondering why the fuck these people are running around singing and dancing when they're all practically on death row-- but not once are you led to believe that the movie is anything but surreal. It completely sucks you into a weird, concocted little world where pretty much anything is possible, but it still stays moderately grounded in reality. Lawyers still act like skeevy scumballs, the media is just as rabid as before, and people are equally stupid as they are in real life, if not more so. What makes the movie succeed is that it amps up every one of these aspects to unbelievable levels, and then allows you to realize that no, they're not that unbelievable after all.

The acting is solid, most surprisingly from Gere, whose nose often ends up simulating an echo chamber whenever he talks. Zellweger isn't a particularly strong lead, but she plays the part of the dumb airheaded blonde quite well. Her character is like the Kim Kardassian of her day, except it just so happens that she's on trial for murder. She shamelessly sells herself, but what really drew me into the character was the fact that she honestly didn't care about her reputation. She had reached the point of complete desperation, and when people have nothing to lose, they do some pretty unbelievable things. All the style and flair to this movie amps the events up to an unrealistic level, but the story at its core isn't all that improbable. And the musical numbers are admittedly great. I'm honestly shocked by how strong the songs were.

Final Score for Chicago: A non-sarcastic and completely surprising 7/10 stars. Yeah, it could have been better. You can say that for most movies, but Chicago really did have more potential than it lived up to. The shallowness of the story can get a little boring, and although we're rooting for Zellweger's character, we certainly don't like her very much. If I were expecting this movie to be on the level of Fight Club, I probably wouldn't have liked it much, but because I went in with low expectations (this is an Oscar-winning musical recommended by Jed, for fuck's sake), I found myself thoroughly entertained. Even if you don't like musicals, I recommend this film. You might be surprised by how much you enjoy yourself.

Movie musicals are, without a doubt, one of the riskiest types of films to approach. Most often they disappoint, with them never getting close to reaching the standard of the source material and the seemingly obligatory casting of A-listers detracting from the music. We had these problems with so many of these movie musicals; Les Miserables, Mamma Mia!, Into the Woods etc etc. But, 2002 Oscar Best Picture Winner, Chicago is a very different story. Now, this movie surprised me. I truly didn't expect it to be as good as it is (perhaps because of the movie musical track record) but Chicago successfully pulls this genre off with flair and artistry. What is the biggest blessing is casting; Renee Zelwegger, Catherine Zeta-Jones, Richard Gere, Queen Latifah, John C.Reilly and all the rest are all not just competent, but actually very good singers who understand the music and perform it with conviction and punch. The film's score is also fantastically jazzy and really helps to turn Chicago from good to great, with a swing score that captures the feel of this Vaudeville musical perfectly. As a whole, this film is delightfully Vaudevillian, with reality merging with cabaret stage, in which our lawyers and murderesses are all performing. This technique is risky, but it is effectively executed, never feeling forced and helping to enhance the story. My one criticism is the film is almost too faithful to the Broadway musical, which it its bane, as it is never going to reach the heights of Chicago on-stage, no matter how hard it tries. Ah, the limits of celluloid. For the film to reach its full potential, it needed to adjust and bring something newer to the production that Broadway didn't. Overall, however, Chicago is a surprising gem of a film, that never loses its roots of showbiz and musical theatre, yet provides us with a bombastic production that truly encompasses "all that jazz"

Musicals aren't generally my thing but in watching every Best Picture winner ever I will have to tackle My Fair Lady (1964), An American in Paris (1951), Oliver! (1968), Going My Way (1944), Gigi (1958), The Great Ziegfeld (1936), The Broadway Melody (1929), West Side Story (1961) and The Sound of Music (1965) but today I'm reviewing 2003's Best Picture winner Chicago. This was not one I was looking forward to as I dreaded watching a group of overly-indulged theatre kids grown up performing a cringe worthy set of overly elaborate dance numbers. Fortunately at least half of the song and dance numbers are pretty great and Catherine Zeta-Jones, Richard Gere when he's not dancing and Christine Baranski are good enough to patch over Renee Zellweger's weak lead performance. Did this deserve to even be nominated at the Academy Awards, hell no! Divorced from it's overpraising it's a decent musical and although I would change many things director Rob Marshall did a great job.

Roxie Hart, Renee Zellweger, is obsessed with fame and the man she has pinned her hopes on is Fred Casely, Dominic West, whom she believes has connections in the entertainment business. When he reveals that he lied she shoots and initially her husband Amos, John C. Reilly, is happy to defend her but when he discovers her infidelity she is sent straight to prison. Velma Kelly, Catherine Zeta-Jones, is a dancer that Roxie witnessed the night of the shooting who also ends up in prison for shooting her husband and sister, also engaging in infidelity. The two women then vie for the attentions of powerful lawyer Billy Flynn, Richard Gere, who uses the power of publicity and press attention to get his clients off. Hart succeeds in her attempts to capture the public consciousness and as she continues to attain press attention with her increasingly desperate claims we see just how phony society is.

The worst parts of the film to me are those that come with all musicals. It's ridiculous to see dancers and singers taking themselves so seriously as they cavort around in an obviously contrived scene. Beyond this however Zellweger is fatally miscast in the lead role as she is not attractive enough to believably catch the eyes of jury members and lacks the singing and dancing abilities to carry off some of the biggest songs in the film. Zellweger was enjoyable as a supporting player in Jerry Maguire (1996) and One True Thing (1998) but during her time as a major star in the early 2000s only Down with Love (2003) managed to use her correctly, I haven't seen Nurse Betty (2000) I'm sorry. Gere is cast well as the slippery lawyer and does some of the best acting in the film within the coutroom scenes but he ruins every song and dance number he has, he just doesn't fit, I don't know who to cast in this role but it certainly isn't Gere. The film as a whole is just shoddily made in some places, too many cuts, which decreased some of it's effect.

The song numbers that I did enjoy were "All That Jazz" and "Mr. Cellophane" which were performed by the ravishing Zeta-Jones and the unlikely musical talent Reilly. The opening number, All That Jazz sets what should be the tone for the entire film as Zeta-Jones is sexy, mysterious and deliberate and pulls off the dancing with aplomb. The song itself it's catchy and puts you in a fun, frenzied mood, exactly how you should feel during a musical. "Mr. Cellophane" is the only time that the film is able to grapple with serious drama successfully. Reilly isn't the best singer and dancer in the world but neither is his character and his sad, pudgy little face is a perfect fit for the song's lyrics about feeling as though people look through him and not at him. If only there was more of this in film I kept thinking as Velma is criminally underused and we spend the majority of our time with unlikable characters portrayed by miscast actors.

If you love musicals this will obviously be for you as Chicago is one of the most notable musicals of the last 50 years and this is from what I understand a faithful adaptation. If you aren't into musicals then you'll already know to stay away but if you're like me and have a secret love for Grease 2 (1982) and Cossacks of the Kuban (1950) the film features two great musical numbers and a great performance from Zeta-Jones, you'll have to watch it in the right mood. When Chicago won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 2002, it was the first musical to do since 1968; musicals had gone out of fashion and Chicago was one of a handful that made them popular again. That's a good thing if you like musicals, but generally speaking I don't. To an extent, this is usually because I don't like the musical genres involved, but I also find it difficult to engage with a narrative when the characters keep bursting into song in the middle of events. Characterisation and story inevitably play second fiddle to the big selling point, which is the singing and associated dancing; what plot musicals have is usually slight. Inherently non-realistic, these films succeed almost purely by delivering entertaining spectacle. And that is something that Chicago has plenty of.
Based on the Broadway musical, Chicago's necessarily economic story is about women murderers in the titular town during the nineteen-twenties. It's surprisingly dark subject matter, featuring several murders and an execution by hanging, and the screenplay deals with this by keeping its tongue firmly in its cheek. As a result, the film is often quite funny, especially during the courtroom scene. Interestingly, director Rob Marshall (in his movie debut) deviates from the stage version by making all of the musical numbers take place in Roxie's imagination, with the exceptions of those that the characters perform on stage at the beginning and end of the film: it's a subtle distinction, but it acknowledges the absurdity I tend to associate with musicals.
What it doesn't do however, is make Chicago more realistic. Marshall doesn't even try: musicals are as much a product of the theatre as they are of cinema, and he embraces the inherent theatricality of the format. When it needs to, the film looks like a convincing recreation of Chicago in the nineteen-twenties thanks to its detailed sets, props and costumes. But when the musical numbers are being performed, Marshall opts for sets that look like they've been made for the Broadway stages sets on which the musical was original performed. On occasion, the juxtaposition is used for dramatic effect, for example when the camera keeps cutting between Katalin Helinszki's actual hanging and a stage-set "vanishing act" version. Later, when lawyer Billy Flynn is defending Roxie Hart in court, the same juxtaposition is used for comic effect, as Flynn's energetic speech is intercut with shots of him tap dancing in an empty theatre.
Marshall assembled an impressive cast for Chicago, including Renée Zellweger as Roxie Hart, Catherine Zeta-Jones as Velma Kelly, and Richard Gere as Billy Flynn, as well as Queen Latifah, Lucy Liu, John C. Reilly and Dominic West. In a production such as this, theatrical, non-naturalistic performances are the order of the day (although Reilly manages to be naturalistic even when he's singing) and the actors deliver larger-than-life turns with considerable charisma and style. Gere's is especially impressive, because this isn't the sort of film one expects to see him in, and his commitment is demonstrated by the fact that he learned to tap-dance for the role. Zellweger and Zeta-Jones give performances that reflect their characters' competition for the limelight and they do so with apparent glee.
As well as directing, Marshall choreographed the film, and the song and dance routines look technically impressive even to a viewer who wouldn't normally choose to listen to this sort of music. There some ingenious touches: when Velma is recounting how she ended up in prison, the eroticism of the dancing and the performers' revealing costumes in the accompanying musical performance ("Cell Block Tango") reflect the sexually-motivated nature of the crimes of the women, whilst also – fittingly – recalling the femme fatales of film noir. Cinematographer Dion Beebe provides dynamic camerawork with a mix of camera angles and whip-pans that are then cut together in the editing room such that the image on-screen changes with a speed appropriate to the rhythm of the music. During the opening stage performance of "All That Jazz", the camera also cuts between the musical number as it rises to a climax and close-up shots of a sex scene as it rises to an entirely different sort of climax. 
Chicago was never going to engage me emotionally. But as a technical achievement, it is impressive and is made with a confidence that shows in every aspect on screen. Little wonder then that it was so popular and is credited with contributing to a renewed interest in musicals at the start of this century.

"Chicago" Review: Killing for Headlines
By Chelli Lopez

"Chicago" takes place in the 1920s where housewife Roxie Hart (played by Renée Zellweger) dreams of being on stage and seeking fame. Roxie ends up going to Murderess Row after killing her secret love affair Fred Casely (played by Dominic West), where she ends up meeting her idol Velma Kelly (played by Catherine Zeta-Jones) who just recently killed her husband and sister. The two end up forming a rivalry after lawyer Billy Flynn (played by Richard Gere) takes on both of their cases where they fight for fame and their names in the headlines. This film ran for 1h and 40m and is available on HBO Max.
The film "Chicago" illustrates beautiful performances that connect well within each scene of the film. The performances act as an insight on what these characters are thinking and simply develop the scene in a  more dramatic and elaborate way. "The Cell Block Tango" was one of those captivating performances that really captured the essence of the film and its characters. The dark stage with only cell bars keeps you in the setting of the Cook County Jail, but the striking red used as a symbol of their dead lovers drives the significance of the performance as the story is told by the six merry murderesses. Catherine Zeta-Jones (Velma Kelly), Susan Misner (Liz), Deidre Goodwin (June), Denise Faye (Annie), Ekaterina Chtchelkanova (Hunyak), and Mya Harrison (Mona) all performed in "The Cell Block Tango". Catherine Zeta-Jones is a welsh actress known for her film career and humanitarian work. Catherine has won many awards such as an Academy Award, a British Academy Film Award, and a Tony award. She is also the Commander of the Order of the British Empire. Susan Misner is an American actress and dancer who has guest starred on many TV shows including the Law And Order franchise. Misner has recently been in The Americans as the role of Sandra Beeman and The Good Wife as the role of Simon Canning. Deidre Goodwin is an American actress who is known for her roles in Chicago, Half Nelson, and Across the Universe. Goodwin is also a musical theater actress and serves on the faculty of New York Film Academy. Denise Faye is an American actress, dancer, choreographer, and director. Faye has won many awards such as the American Choreography Award, and the Screen Actors Guild Award for the 2002 film "Chicago".  Ekaterina Chtchelkanova is a Russian ballerina, singer, and actress best known for her role in "Chicago" as Hunyak. She appeared with Les Grands Ballets Canadiens de Montréal in 2008 and founded the Open World Dance Foundation in 2010. Mya Harrison is an American singer, songwriter, actress and dancer. Mya is an independent R&B and Pop artist who has won and been nominated for many Grammy Awards. Another outstanding performance was the "Hungarian Disappearing Act". This performance was extremely emotional but executed in such a captivating way. Hunyak performed in a packed house being introduced to the audience for their "pleasure and entertainment". Hunyaks performance captured the attention of everyone in Chicago because she was the first woman to be executed in the state of Illinois. Her packed house that was full of applause and standing ovations when she was hung connected to the story's dramatic and quick turn of events. Her execution was a main story in the headlines, but once she was dead no one gave her a second thought.
The director and choreographer of the film "Chicago" is Rob Marshall. Rob Marshall is an American director, producer, and choreographer who works in both theater and film. He is most known for helming the motion picture adaptation of the Broadway musical Chicago. He received nominations for the Academy Award for Best Director, the Golden Globe Award for Best Director, and the BAFTA Award for Best Direction for his work on the movie, which also won him the Directors Guild of America Award for Outstanding Directing - Feature Film. Prior to his directing career he started as a dancer for various Broadway productions but suffered a herniated disc while performing in "Cats". The story and the narrative became very clear after  Roxie Hart (played by Renée Zellweger) killed her love affair  Fred Casely (played by Dominic West). The escalation from when Fred told Roxie that he never talked to any guy and that she would never be a star, to then Roxie shooting him dead gives an insight to the viewers that the events in this story are as dramatic as they are fast, with one minute Roxie being famous for killing her love affair, to now Kitty (played by Lucy Liu) being famous for murdering her husband and his two mistresses. The director also captures the selfishness in Roxie beautifully, from her song about her husband called "Funny Hunny", down to her faking her pregnancy and lying to her husband just for one for minute in the headlines. The narrative was staged precisely, allowing viewers to connect and feel sympathy for the women on death row, while also showing why these dysfunctional women are kept on death row for their heinous crimes against men. Connecting the musical performances to the corresponding scenes was done very effectively. It gave a greater understanding of what was happening throughout the story. This was done nicely during the opening number of "All That Jazz" corresponding to Roxie and Freds love scene and to Hunyaks' "Hungarian Disappearing Act".  
The production team for "Chicago" consisted of production designer John Myhre, art director Andrew Stearn, and Colleen Atwood in costumes. John Myhre is an American production designer who has been employed by Hollywood since the late 1980s. He became the forefront of Hollywood production designers in 1998 when Shekhar Kapur's Elizabeth earned him his first Academy Award nomination for Best Art Direction. Andrew Stearn is a producer who is known for his work in "Shameless" and "The West Wing". Colleen Atwood is an American costume designer who has won four times out of her twelve nominations for the Academy Award for Best Costume Design, including for the movies Chicago, Memoirs of a Geisha, Alice in Wonderland, and Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them. The production design in "Chicago" was executed very successfully. They brought out the glitz and glamor of the club life in Chicago, while also showing the dark and dirty parts of living in Chicago. The music fit perfectly with the setting and time period being in 1920s Chicago. I enjoyed seeing African Americans in the jazz band with Taye Diggs being the bandleader. During that time the first and most famous jazz players were African Americans, so making the jazz band an all African American group fit really well with the time period of this film.
My overall opinion of this film is positive. With the film being close to two hours, it sure went by fast. "Chicago" had amazing directing that told the story very admirably. The story was fairly simple to understand, however the musical performances that corresponded with the scenes may cause some confusion to new viewers. Overall this film was very well executed and I can positively say "Chicago" is definitely worth watching.

There are some really eye-catching visuals in here ("We Both Reached For The Gun" and "Roxie" have my personal favorites), so all-in-all, it's a very enjoyable evening for anyone not opposed to some salacious razzle-dazzle.
